lessons.title: Common Soybean Diseases: Rust, Blight, Root Rot
lessons.body:
Soybean rust is the most feared disease in Africa. It starts as tiny brown or reddish-brown spots on the underside of leaves. These spots have raised pustules that release spores. In humid conditions, rust can spread across a field in 7 to 10 days and cause 30% to 80% yield loss. Scout your field twice a week from flowering onwards. Look under leaves, especially lower and middle canopy. If you find rust on 5 out of 100 plants, spray a fungicide immediately.

Blight comes in two main forms: bacterial blight and frogeye leaf spot. Bacterial blight causes angular, water-soaked spots that turn brown with a yellow halo. It spreads through rain splash and infected seed. Frogeye leaf spot causes small, circular spots with gray centers and dark brown borders. It thrives in warm, wet weather. Both blights reduce pod fill and seed quality. Remove crop residue after harvest and use certified disease-free seed.

Root rot is caused by soil fungi like Rhizoctonia and Pythium. Plants wilt suddenly even when soil is moist. Pull a wilted plant and look at the roots: they will be brown or black instead of creamy white. Root rot is worst in poorly drained soils and when soybeans are planted after soybeans. Rotate with maize or sorghum for at least two seasons. Improve drainage by making ridges or planting on raised beds. Treat seed with a fungicide like metalaxyl before planting.

Other common diseases include downy mildew, which causes yellow patches on upper leaves and fuzzy gray growth underneath, and anthracnose, which causes dark lesions on stems and pods. All these diseases reduce yield and seed quality. The key is early detection and quick action. Walk your field in a zigzag pattern, checking 20 plants in 5 different spots. Keep records of what you see and when. This helps you choose the right control method next season.

lessons.title: Disease Identification and Diagnosis
lessons.body:
To identify soybean diseases correctly, you need to look at three things: symptoms on leaves, symptoms on stems and pods, and symptoms on roots. Start by checking lower leaves first because many diseases start there. Use a hand lens (10x magnification) to see fungal structures like pustules or spores. Take photos with your phone and compare with online guides or ask your extension officer.

For leaf diseases: Rust shows small, raised, reddish-brown pustules on the underside. Downy mildew shows pale yellow spots on top and grayish fuzz underneath. Bacterial blight shows angular spots with yellow halos. Frogeye leaf spot shows round spots with gray centers and dark borders. Viral diseases like soybean mosaic cause mottled, puckered leaves and distorted pods. Note the pattern: are spots scattered or in patches? Are they on older or newer leaves?

For stem and pod diseases: Anthracnose causes dark, sunken lesions on stems and pods. Pod and stem blight causes black specks (pycnidia) in rows on stems. Charcoal rot causes gray streaks inside stems when split open. When you split a stem, look for brown discoloration in the pith. That often means root rot or stem rot has moved up.

For root diseases: Carefully dig up a wilted plant with a fork, keeping roots intact. Wash roots in water. Healthy roots are white to light brown. Diseased roots are dark brown, black, or mushy. Root rot fungi often cause the outer root layer to slip off easily. Nodules on roots should be pink inside if they are fixing nitrogen. If nodules are green or brown, they are not working.

Keep a simple notebook. For each problem, write the date, field location, crop stage, symptoms, and weather. This record helps you and your extension officer decide whether to spray, rotate, or change varieties. If you are unsure, send a photo to a plant clinic or use a diagnosis app like Plantix. Early and correct diagnosis saves money and prevents yield loss.

lessons.title: Fungicide Application and Timing
lessons.body:
Fungicides are chemicals that kill or stop fungal diseases. They work best when applied before the disease spreads widely. For soybean rust, the critical time is from flowering (R1) to pod fill (R5). If you see rust on 5% of leaves, spray within 24 to 48 hours. Do not wait. Use a knapsack sprayer with a flat fan nozzle. Spray the undersides of leaves because that is where rust pustules are. Walk at a steady pace and keep the nozzle 30 to 40 cm above the canopy.

Choose the right fungicide. For rust, use a triazole (e.g., tebuconazole) or a strobilurin (e.g., azoxystrobin). Mix according to label instructions. A common rate is 0.5 to 1 liter per hectare in 200 to 300 liters of water. For root rot, seed treatment is better than spraying. For blight, use copper-based fungicides or chlorothalonil. Always wear protective clothing: gloves, mask, long sleeves, and boots. Never spray in strong wind or when rain is expected within 6 hours.

Timing is everything. Spray at first sign of disease. If weather stays wet and warm (25-30Â°C), spray again after 14 days. Do not spray more than three times per season to avoid resistance. Rotate fungicide groups: use a triazole first, then a strobilurin, then a different mode of action. This prevents fungi from becoming resistant. Also, spray early in the morning or late afternoon to avoid leaf burn and to protect bees.

Calibrate your sprayer before use. Measure a 10 m by 10 m area (100 mÂ²). Fill sprayer with water and spray that area. Measure how much water you used. If you used 2 liters, then for 1 hectare (10,000 mÂ²) you need 200 liters. Adjust walking speed or nozzle size to get the right volume. Clean your sprayer after each use with soap and water. Store chemicals in a locked cabinet away from children and food. Proper application saves crops and money.

lessons.title: Resistant Varieties and Genetic Control
lessons.body:
The cheapest and safest way to control soybean diseases is to plant resistant varieties. Resistance means the plant can fight off or tolerate a disease. For soybean rust, look for varieties with resistance genes like Rpp1, Rpp2, Rpp3, Rpp4, or Rpp5. In Africa, many improved varieties from IITA (International Institute of Tropical Agriculture) have some resistance. Examples include TGx 1835-10E, TGx 1987-62F, and SC Saga. Ask your seed supplier for a variety description sheet that lists disease resistance.

For bacterial blight, resistance is also available. Varieties like TGx 1448-2E and TGx 1740-2F show good tolerance. For frogeye leaf spot, look for varieties with resistance to Cercospora sojina. For root rot, no variety is fully resistant, but some tolerate poorly drained soils better. Always choose varieties that are recommended for your agro-ecological zone. A variety that resists rust in Nigeria may not resist the same rust strain in Uganda.

Genetic control also includes using certified seed. Certified seed is tested for seed-borne diseases like bacterial blight and anthracnose. Do not save seed from a diseased crop. If you must save seed, only save from healthy plants and treat it before planting. Plant multiple varieties with different resistance genes. This is called diversity. If one variety fails due to a new disease strain, others may survive. Do not plant the same variety on your whole farm.

Breeding new varieties takes time, but you can help. Report new or unusual disease symptoms to your extension officer or research station. They may use your report to breed better varieties. Also, rotate resistant varieties every 3 to 4 years. Diseases can overcome resistance if you use the same variety continuously. Combine resistant varieties with good sanitation and crop rotation. No single method works alone. Integrated disease management gives the best results.

lessons.title: Sanitation and Crop Rotation for Disease Prevention
lessons.body:
Sanitation means keeping your field clean of disease sources. After harvest, remove or destroy crop residues. Many fungi and bacteria survive in old leaves and stems. If you leave them, they will infect your next soybean crop. You can plough residues into the soil, burn them (only if allowed), or feed them to livestock after drying. Do not dump diseased residues near your field. Clean your tools and boots before moving to another field. Wash with soap and water or spray with 70% alcohol.

Crop rotation is the practice of planting different crops in a sequence. For soybean diseases, rotate with cereals like maize, sorghum, or millet. These crops are not hosts for soybean rust, blight, or root rot. A good rotation is: Year 1 â maize, Year 2 â soybean, Year 3 â sorghum, Year 4 â soybean. This breaks the disease cycle. Do not plant soybean after soybean. Also avoid planting soybean after other legumes like cowpea or groundnut because they share some diseases.

Rotation works because many pathogens cannot survive without a host. For example, soybean rust needs living soybean plants to survive. If you plant maize for one season, rust spores die. Root rot fungi can survive in soil for 2 to 3 years, so a 2-year break from soybean is better. If you have a small farm, rotate in strips or beds. Even a 10-meter wide strip of maize between soybean plots can reduce disease spread.

Other sanitation practices: control weeds because some weeds host diseases. Remove volunteer soybean plants that grow from previous seed. These can carry diseases. Use clean, certified seed. If you use manure, compost it well to kill pathogens. Keep your field free of standing water by making drainage channels. Do not work in the field when leaves are wet because you can spread bacteria. Follow these practices every season. They cost little but prevent major losses.

lessons.title: Seed Treatment for Disease Control
lessons.body:
Seed treatment means coating seeds with fungicides, insecticides, or other chemicals before planting. It protects the seed and young seedling from soil-borne and seed-borne diseases. Many soybean diseases, like root rot, bacterial blight, and anthracnose, start from infected seed or soil. Treating seed is cheap and effective. You can treat seed yourself or buy pre-treated seed. Always check the label for the correct product and rate.

Common seed treatment fungicides include metalaxyl, mefenoxam, fludioxonil, and thiram. For root rot (Pythium and Phytophthora), metalaxyl is very effective. For Rhizoctonia and Fusarium, use fludioxonil or thiram. A combination product like Apron XL (metalaxyl) plus Maxim (fludioxonil) gives broad protection. The rate is usually 2 to 5 ml per kilogram of seed. Mix with a small amount of water (10-15 ml per kg seed) to make a slurry. Pour over seed in a bucket or drum. Stir well until all seeds are coated evenly. Let dry in shade before planting.

You can also use biological seed treatments. These contain beneficial fungi or bacteria like Trichoderma or Bacillus. They are safe for humans and the environment. Mix 5 to 10 grams of powder per kilogram of seed. Biologicals work best when combined with good sanitation. For insect pests like bean fly, add an insecticide like imidacloprid at 3 to 5 ml per kg seed. Never mix fungicide and insecticide unless the label says it is safe.

Safety first. Wear gloves, mask, and long sleeves when treating seed. Do not eat, drink, or smoke during treatment. Treat seed in a well-ventilated area. Store treated seed in a labeled bag away from food and animal feed. Do not use treated seed for human consumption or animal feed. Plant treated seed within 2 to 3 weeks. If you buy pre-treated seed, check the color (usually pink or green) and the expiration date. Proper seed treatment gives your soybean crop a strong start and reduces the need for later sprays.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Disease Management in African Soybean Farming

Soybean is one of Africa's fastest-growing cash and food crops. From Nigeria's middle belt to Zambia's plateau, from South Africa's Highveld to Uganda's northern districts, soybean now anchors smallholder and commercial rotations alike. But yield losses from disease routinely reach 20â40% in untreated fields, and up to 80% where rust strikes early and no fungicide is applied. For the agribusiness operator â whether you farm 2 hectares or 200 â disease management is not an agronomic footnote. It is a profit-and-loss line item.

This Practical Reference consolidates the core decision points from the Disease Management module: identifying the major diseases (rust, blight, root rot), diagnosing them correctly, timing fungicide applications for return on investment, selecting resistant varieties, using sanitation and rotation, and treating seed before planting. Treat it as a field-side checklist, not a textbook.

1. Know the Three Priority Diseases

Soybean rust (Phakopsora pachyrhizi) is the single greatest foliar threat across sub-Saharan Africa. It spreads by wind-borne spores, can defoliate a field in 3â4 weeks, and causes yield losses of 10â80%. Scout weekly from flowering. Look for tiny tan-to-reddish-brown pustules on the underside of leaves.

Blight (including bacterial blight and Cercospora leaf blight) appears as angular brown lesions with yellow halos, usually starting in the lower canopy. It thrives in humid, warm conditions and can reduce seed quality and pod fill.

Root rot (caused by Rhizoctonia, Pythium, Fusarium, and Phytophthora species) attacks the root system and stem base. Plants wilt in patches, often after heavy rain or in compacted, poorly drained soils. Once symptoms are visible above ground, yield loss is already locked in.

2. Disease Identification and Diagnosis

Correct diagnosis determines whether you spend money on fungicide or save it. The table below is your first-line decision tool.

Table 1: Field diagnosis of common soybean diseases
Disease Key symptoms Conditions favouring it Look-alike / confusion
Soybean rust Small reddish-brown pustules on leaf underside; yellowing; early defoliation Warm, humid; 15â28Â°C; wind-borne spread Frogeye leaf spot (larger, grey-centred lesions)
Bacterial blight Angular, water-soaked lesions with yellow halos; leaves tear easily Warm, wet weather; wind-driven rain Cercospora blight (more purple-brown, less angular)
Cercospora leaf blight Purple-brown leathery lesions on upper leaves; seed staining High humidity; warm nights Rust (pustules vs. flat lesions)
Root rot complex Dark, rotted roots; wilted patches; stunted plants; stem base discolouration Waterlogged or compacted soils; cool, wet planting Nutrient deficiency (patchy but no root rot)

Source: IITA Soybean Disease Management Guide (2022); CABI Crop Protection Compendium (2023).

3. Fungicide Application and Timing

Fungicides only pay when applied at the right growth stage. For rust, the critical window is R1 (beginning flowering) to R3 (beginning pod). Application after R5 rarely recovers yield. Use a triazole + strobilurin mix where available; rotate modes of action to slow resistance.

Table 2: Fungicide timing and expected return
Growth stage Action Expected yield protection Notes
VEâV5 (vegetative) Scout only; no spray unless root rot confirmed â Seed treatment covers early root disease
R1âR2 (flowering) First fungicide if rust detected or high risk 15â30% Best ROI window
R3âR4 (pod development) Second application if disease pressure continues 10â20% Respect pre-harvest interval
R5âR6 (seed fill) Generally not economic <5% Spray only if rust arrives late and crop is high-value

Source: IITA Integrated Soybean Disease Management (2022); Syngenta agronomy guidance for African soybean systems (2023).

â  SAFETY WARNING â FUNGICIDE HANDLING

Always wear a long-sleeved shirt, trousers, closed shoes, gloves, and a face mask when mixing or spraying fungicides. Never eat, drink, or smoke during application. Store chemicals in a locked, labelled container away from food, children, and livestock. Observe the pre-harvest interval on the label â spraying too close to harvest leaves illegal residues and can destroy your buyer contract. Dispose of empty containers through certified collection points; never reuse them for water or food.

4. Resistant Varieties and Genetic Control

Variety choice is the cheapest disease-control investment you will ever make. In Africa, publicly released varieties with rust tolerance or resistance include TGx lines from IITA and national programme releases in Nigeria, Zambia, Malawi, and Uganda. Resistance is rarely absolute â it delays infection and reduces severity, buying you time and reducing fungicide frequency.

For root rot, genetic resistance to Phytophthora is well documented in certain varieties; ask your seed supplier for the resistance profile. For bacterial blight, resistant varieties plus clean seed are the primary control, since no chemical cure exists.

5. Sanitation and Crop Rotation

Disease inoculum survives in crop residue, soil, and volunteer plants. Practical sanitation steps:

  • Remove or plough in infected residue after harvest where root rot is present.
  • Rotate soybean with a non-host cereal (maize, sorghum, millet) for at least one season â two is better where root rot is severe.
  • Control volunteer soybean plants between seasons; they carry rust and blight.
  • Clean implements between fields to avoid moving infested soil.
  • Improve drainage in low-lying patches to reduce root rot pressure.

6. Seed Treatment for Disease Control

Seed treatment protects the seedling during the first 2â4 weeks, the period when root rot and damping-off cause the most stand loss. Use a fungicide seed treatment (e.g., metalaxyl + thiram or a registered equivalent) plus an inoculant for nitrogen fixation. Treat seed only with approved products, and never mix inoculant and fungicide in the same tank unless the label confirms compatibility â fungicides can kill Rhizobium bacteria.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Scout fields weekly from emergence; intensify from R1.
  2. Identify disease correctly before spending on chemicals â use Table 1.
  3. Spray rust at R1âR3, not later; rotate fungicide modes of action.
  4. Choose a variety with documented rust and root rot resistance.
  5. Treat seed with approved fungicide plus compatible inoculant.
  6. Rotate with cereals for at least one season after a disease-heavy crop.
  7. Manage residue and volunteers to break the disease cycle.
  8. Record every spray: date, product, rate, stage, and result â this drives next season's budget.

Further Reading

  • IITA â Soybean Research and Disease Management Resources
  • CABI Crop Protection Compendium â Soybean Disease Datasheets
  • FAO â Soybean Production and Protection Guidance
  • American Phytopathological Society â Disease Diagnosis Resources
  • IITA â Soybean Disease Management Guide (PDF)

Business takeaway: Every dollar spent on the right variety, clean seed, and correctly timed fungicide returns two to five dollars in protected yield. Every dollar spent on the wrong product at the wrong stage returns nothing. Diagnose first, then spend.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of soybean rust?
options: A) White fuzzy growth on stems
B) Tiny reddish-brown pustules on the underside of leaves
C) Yellowing of the whole plant
quiz.explanation: Soybean rust starts as small, raised, reddish-brown pustules on the lower leaf surface.

quiz.q: Which disease causes angular, water-soaked spots with a yellow halo?
quiz.explanation: Bacterial blight is characterized by angular, water-soaked spots that turn brown with a yellow halo.

quiz.q: What is a key symptom of root rot in soybean?
options: A) Bright orange pustules on leaves
B) Wilting plants with brown or black roots
C) White powdery growth on pods
quiz.explanation: Root rot causes sudden wilting even in moist soil, and roots become brown or black instead of creamy white.

quiz.q: Which crop is a good rotation partner to break soybean disease cycles?
quiz.explanation: Maize is a cereal and not a host for major soybean diseases, so it helps break disease cycles.

quiz.q: When should you spray fungicide for soybean rust?
options: B) When you see rust on 5 out of 100 plants
quiz.explanation: The threshold for spraying rust is when 5% of plants show symptoms, and action should be taken within 24-48 hours.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to check for root rot?
options: B) Pull a wilted plant and examine roots
C) Spray the field with water
D) Count the number of pods
quiz.explanation: Root rot is diagnosed by digging up a wilted plant and checking if roots are brown or black instead of healthy white.

quiz.q: Which fungicide group is commonly used for soybean rust?
quiz.explanation: Triazoles (e.g., tebuconazole) and strobilurins are effective against soybean rust.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spray volume per hectare for soybean fungicide?
quiz.explanation: A common spray volume for ground application is 200 to 300 liters of water per hectare.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate fungicide groups?
quiz.explanation: Rotating fungicide modes of action prevents fungi from developing resistance to a single chemical.

quiz.q: Which of these is a resistant variety for soybean rust?
options: C) Any variety from the market
D) A variety with no label
quiz.explanation: TGx 1835-10E is an improved variety from IITA that carries resistance to soybean rust.

quiz.q: What does Rpp1 stand for?
options: B) A resistance gene for soybean rust
quiz.explanation: Rpp genes are resistance genes that help soybean plants fight off rust.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation important for disease control?
options: B) It breaks the disease cycle by starving pathogens
D) It makes plants grow taller
quiz.explanation: Rotating to non-host crops reduces pathogen populations because they cannot survive without a host.

quiz.q: What should you do with diseased crop residues after harvest?
options: A) Leave them on the field
C) Spread them on healthy fields
quiz.explanation: Removing or destroying residues eliminates sources of fungal and bacterial inoculum.

quiz.q: Which seed treatment fungicide is effective against Pythium root rot?
quiz.explanation: Metalaxyl (or mefenoxam) is specifically effective against Pythium and Phytophthora root rots.

quiz.q: What is the typical rate for seed treatment fungicide per kg of soybean seed?
quiz.explanation: Most seed treatment fungicides are applied at 2 to 5 milliliters per kilogram of seed.

quiz.q: Why should you wear protective clothing when treating seed?
quiz.explanation: Seed treatment chemicals can be toxic, so gloves, mask, and long sleeves prevent skin contact and inhalation.

quiz.q: Which disease is NOT controlled by crop rotation with maize?
quiz.explanation: Root rot fungi can survive in soil for 2-3 years, so a single season of maize may not fully control them.

quiz.q: What is a sign of healthy nitrogen-fixing nodules on soybean roots?
quiz.explanation: Active nodules have a pink or red interior due to the presence of leghaemoglobin, indicating nitrogen fixation.

quiz.q: Which tool is useful for identifying fungal structures on leaves?
quiz.explanation: A 10x hand lens allows you to see pustules, spores, and other fungal structures clearly.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find rust on 10% of plants?
options: A) Wait for it to dry
quiz.explanation: Rust spreads quickly; spraying immediately when threshold is exceeded prevents major yield loss.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biological seed treatment?
quiz.explanation: Trichoderma is a beneficial fungus used as a biological seed treatment to protect against pathogens.

quiz.q: Why should you clean your sprayer after use?
options: A) To prevent chemical residues from damaging next crop
B) To make it look new
quiz.explanation: Residues of one chemical can harm a different crop or cause resistance if not properly cleaned.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to spray fungicide?
options: A) Midday when sun is hottest
B) Early morning or late afternoon
quiz.explanation: Spraying in early morning or late afternoon reduces leaf burn and protects pollinators.

quiz.q: How many times per season should you spray fungicide to avoid resistance?
options: A) As many as you want
B) No more than three times
quiz.explanation: Limiting sprays to no more than three per season and rotating chemicals reduces resistance risk.

quiz.q: Which symptom is typical of downy mildew?
options: B) Yellow patches on upper leaves with gray fuzz underneath
quiz.explanation: Downy mildew causes pale yellow spots on the top of leaves and fuzzy gray growth on the underside.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to prevent bacterial blight?
quiz.explanation: Bacterial blight is seed-borne, so using certified disease-free seed is a key prevention method.

quiz.q: Which of these is a symptom of anthracnose?
options: A) Dark sunken lesions on stems and pods
quiz.explanation: Anthracnose causes dark, sunken lesions on stems, pods, and sometimes leaves.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation with a non-legume important?
options: B) It breaks disease cycles and reduces soil pathogens
D) It makes soybean grow faster
quiz.explanation: Non-legume rotation starves soybean-specific pathogens, reducing disease pressure.

quiz.q: What should you do before planting saved seed?
quiz.explanation: Saved seed can carry diseases, so treating it with fungicide reduces seed-borne infection.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if you see new disease symptoms you don't recognize?
options: B) Report to extension officer or use a diagnosis app
quiz.explanation: Reporting unusual symptoms helps get correct diagnosis and prevents spread; apps like Plantix can assist.
